lessons.title: Vaccination Protocols for Feedlot Steers
lessons.body: Vaccination is your first line of defense against costly disease outbreaks in a feedlot. In Africa, common diseases like blackleg, botulism, and lumpy skin disease can wipe out your profits. Start with a clear protocol: all steers should be vaccinated at arrival, then boostered as needed. For blackleg, use a 7-way clostridial vaccine (e.g., Ultrabac 7) â give 2 ml under the skin. For botulism, use a toxoid vaccine â 5 ml under the skin. For lumpy skin disease, use a live attenuated vaccine â 1 ml under the skin. Always check with a local vet for region-specific diseases. Timing matters: vaccinate healthy animals only. Never vaccinate sick or stressed steers â wait until they recover. Handle vaccines carefully: keep them refrigerated at 2-8Â°C, never freeze. Use clean needles â change every 10-15 animals to avoid abscesses. Record every vaccination: date, product, batch number, and animal ID. In hot climates, vaccinate in the cool of the morning. A good protocol costs about $2-3 per steer but saves thousands in losses. Work with your vet to design a schedule that fits your farmâs disease history.

lessons.title: Common Diseases: Respiratory and Digestive
lessons.body: Respiratory and digestive diseases are the top killers in feedlots. Bovine Respiratory Disease (BRD) causes pneumonia, often triggered by stress from transport or mixing. Signs: rapid breathing, coughing, nasal discharge, droopy ears, and fever above 39.5Â°C. Treat early with antibiotics like oxytetracycline (20 mg/kg body weight) or tulathromycin (2.5 mg/kg). Digestive diseases include bloat and acidosis. Bloat happens when gas builds up in the rumen â left side swells, animal kicks at belly, breathes hard. Treat with a stomach tube or trocar and cannula in emergency. Acidosis from too much grain: symptoms are loose manure, off-feed, and lameness. Prevent by gradually increasing grain over 3 weeks. For both, isolate sick animals immediately. Provide fresh water and good-quality hay. In Africa, plant poisoning (e.g., from Lantana) can mimic these signs â check your pastures. Use a thermometer to confirm fever. Keep a treatment log: animal ID, symptoms, drug used, withdrawal period. Withdrawal periods for meat: oxytetracycline 28 days, tulathromycin 18 days. Never sell animals before withdrawal ends. Early detection and treatment reduce mortality by up to 80%.

lessons.title: Parasite Control: Internal and External
lessons.body: Parasites steal nutrients and cause disease. Internal parasites (worms) like roundworms and liver flukes are common in Africa. Use dewormers: albendazole (7.5 mg/kg) or ivermectin (0.2 mg/kg) under the skin. Deworm every 3-4 months, or when fecal egg counts are high. Collect fresh manure, mix with salt solution, and count eggs under a microscope â your vet can do this. External parasites: ticks, lice, and mange mites. Ticks transmit diseases like heartwater and anaplasmosis. Use tick grease (e.g., amitraz) or spray with cypermethrin every 2 weeks. For mange, inject ivermectin. Rotate chemicals to prevent resistance. Keep pens dry â ticks breed in wet, dirty areas. In hot, humid regions, tick control is critical. Also control flies with traps and hygiene. A good parasite program costs about $1-2 per steer per month but improves weight gain by 10-15%. Always follow withdrawal periods: ivermectin 35 days, albendazole 14 days. Record all treatments. Work with your vet to design a strategic deworming schedule based on your farmâs history and season.

lessons.title: Biosecurity Measures
lessons.body: Biosecurity keeps diseases out of your feedlot. Start with a perimeter fence and a single entry point. Use a footbath with disinfectant (e.g., 2% sodium hypochlorite) at the gate. All visitors must wear clean boots and overalls. Quarantine new animals for 30 days â keep them 50 meters away from the main herd. Test for diseases like brucellosis and tuberculosis before mixing. Clean and disinfect pens, water troughs, and feed bunks weekly. Use a pressure washer and a disinfectant like Virkon. Control rodents and birds â they carry diseases. Store feed in sealed bins. Never share equipment with other farms without disinfecting. When an animal dies, bury it deep (2 meters) or incinerate â never leave carcasses around. Isolate sick animals immediately in a hospital pen. Train workers on hygiene: wash hands, change clothes. In Africa, where many farms are small, simple measures like a dedicated pair of boots and a hand-washing station can make a big difference. A biosecurity plan costs little but prevents outbreaks that can kill 20% of your herd. Write down your plan and review it monthly.

lessons.title: Recognizing Signs of Illness and Early Intervention
lessons.body: Early detection saves lives. Learn to spot sick steers quickly. Key signs: off-feed (not eating at the trough), droopy ears, sunken eyes, rapid breathing, coughing, nasal discharge, diarrhea, lameness, and isolation from the group. Take the animalâs temperature â normal is 38-39Â°C. Fever above 39.5Â°C means infection. Check gum color: pale gums indicate anemia; yellow gums indicate liver problems. Use a simple body condition score: ribs visible = too thin. Walk the pens twice daily, morning and evening. Look for animals lagging behind. When you find a sick steer, move it to a hospital pen immediately. Provide shade, fresh water, and soft hay. Treat according to your vetâs protocol â donât guess. For BRD, start antibiotics early. For diarrhea, give oral rehydration fluids. Keep a daily log: date, animal ID, signs, treatment, and outcome. In Africa, where vet access may be limited, train one worker as a health monitor. A $10 thermometer and a notebook are your best tools. Early intervention can reduce mortality from 10% to under 2%.

lessons.title: Working with Veterinarians and Health Records
lessons.body: A good relationship with a veterinarian is essential. Find a vet who works with cattle and knows your area. Schedule a visit at least once a month, or more if you have outbreaks. Have a written contract: what services, how much, and emergency contact. Your vet can help design vaccination and deworming schedules, diagnose diseases, and prescribe antibiotics. Always follow their prescription â donât use human drugs or guess doses. Keep accurate health records: animal ID, date, disease, treatment, drug, dose, withdrawal period, and cost. Use a simple notebook or a smartphone app like Farmbrite. Records help you track patterns â if pneumonia keeps happening, you can fix ventilation or reduce stress. They also prove to buyers that your meat is safe. For every animal sold, you must know the withdrawal period has passed. In Africa, where formal vet services may be scarce, join a farmer cooperative that shares a vet. Train a worker to keep records daily. Good records reduce drug costs by 20% and improve herd health. Review records monthly with your vet to adjust your plan.

quiz.q: What is the recommended storage temperature for vaccines?
quiz.explanation: Vaccines must be kept refrigerated at 2-8Â°C to maintain potency; freezing or heat destroys them.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is used to prevent blackleg in steers?
quiz.explanation: Blackleg is caused by Clostridium chauvoei, and a 7-way clostridial vaccine provides protection.

quiz.q: How often should you change needles when vaccinating a herd?
quiz.explanation: Changing needles every 10-15 animals reduces the risk of abscesses and disease transmission.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of Bovine Respiratory Disease (BRD)?
options: A) Droopy ears and nasal discharge
quiz.explanation: BRD typically causes respiratory signs like droopy ears, nasal discharge, and coughing.

quiz.q: What is the normal body temperature for a steer?
quiz.explanation: Normal bovine body temperature ranges from 38 to 39Â°C; fever is above 39.5Â°C.

quiz.q: Which drug is used to treat bloat in an emergency?
quiz.explanation: A trocar and cannula is used to release gas from the rumen in severe bloat.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for oxytetracycline in meat?
quiz.explanation: Oxytetracycline has a 28-day withdrawal period before slaughter for human consumption.

quiz.q: Which internal parasite is common in African cattle?
quiz.explanation: Liver flukes are internal parasites that affect cattle, especially in wet areas.

quiz.q: What is the dose of ivermectin for deworming cattle?
quiz.explanation: Ivermectin is given at 0.2 mg per kg body weight, usually by subcutaneous injection.

quiz.q: How often should you treat for external parasites like ticks?
quiz.explanation: Ticks reproduce quickly, so regular treatment every 2 weeks is needed in high-risk areas.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for ivermectin?
quiz.explanation: Ivermectin has a 35-day withdrawal period for meat.

quiz.q: Which of these is a biosecurity measure?
options: B) Quarantining new animals for 30 days
C) Mixing new and old animals immediately
quiz.explanation: Quarantine prevents the introduction of diseases from new animals into the herd.

quiz.q: What disinfectant is recommended for footbaths?
quiz.explanation: A 2% sodium hypochlorite solution is effective and commonly used in footbaths.

quiz.q: How deep should you bury a dead animal?
quiz.explanation: Burying at least 2 meters deep prevents scavengers from digging up carcasses and spreading disease.

quiz.q: What is a sign of acidosis in steers?
quiz.explanation: Acidosis from too much grain causes digestive upset, leading to loose manure and reduced feed intake.

quiz.q: How can you prevent acidosis when introducing grain?
quiz.explanation: Gradual adaptation allows rumen microbes to adjust, preventing acidosis.

quiz.q: What does pale gum color indicate?
quiz.explanation: Pale gums are a sign of anemia, often caused by parasites or blood loss.

quiz.q: How often should you walk the pens to check for sick animals?
quiz.explanation: Walking pens twice daily (morning and evening) helps detect illness early.

quiz.q: What is a good tool for early disease detection?
quiz.explanation: A thermometer helps identify fever, a key indicator of infection.

quiz.q: What should you do first when you find a sick steer?
options: A) Isolate it in a hospital pen
quiz.explanation: Isolating sick animals prevents disease spread and allows for focused care.

quiz.q: How often should a vet visit your feedlot at minimum?
quiz.explanation: Regular monthly visits help maintain herd health and catch problems early.

quiz.q: Why are health records important?
options: A) To track patterns and ensure withdrawal periods
quiz.explanation: Records help identify disease trends and ensure meat is safe for consumption.

quiz.q: What is a sign of lumpy skin disease?
quiz.explanation: Lumpy skin disease causes characteristic skin nodules and fever.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is used for botulism?
quiz.explanation: Botulism is prevented with a toxoid vaccine that stimulates immunity against the toxin.

quiz.q: What is the dose of albendazole for deworming?
quiz.explanation: Albendazole is given orally at 7.5 mg per kg body weight.

quiz.q: What is a common external parasite of cattle?
quiz.explanation: Ticks are external parasites that feed on blood and transmit diseases.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for albendazole?
quiz.explanation: Albendazole has a 14-day withdrawal period for meat.

quiz.q: What should you do with a dead animal?
quiz.explanation: Proper disposal prevents disease spread and protects other animals.

quiz.q: What is a sign of fever in cattle?
quiz.explanation: Fever is defined as a body temperature above 39.5Â°C.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of good health records?
quiz.explanation: Accurate records help optimize treatments and reduce unnecessary drug use.
